paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-2 (FAME2) is an autosomal dominant familial cortical reflex myoclonus. It presents as an action-induced shivering movement of the hands and jerking of the upper limbs (cortical tremor). These are variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. In the commonest form, a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor occurs together with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are uncommon and tend to occur around sleep onset. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and the myoclonus often worsens in advanced age (De Fusco et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2012).

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) reported a pedigree with 8 affected individuals. Their disorder was nonprogressive, with onset between the ages of 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 also had complex partial seizures. Most individuals had rarely had seizures and had a normal cognitive level. However, the 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Electrophysiologic studies showed an enhanced C-reflex at rest and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. On transcranial magnetic stimulation, the resting motor threshold was significantly reduced. The post-MEP silent period was significantly shortened (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). In 5 patients, EEG-EMG coherence at 8 to 25 Hz over the contralateral rolandic area, with EEG preceding EMG by 8 to 15 ms, suggested that the myoclonus was of cortical origin. Ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients suggested transcallosal spread. The authors suggested diffuse cortical hyperexcitability, particularly involving frontotemporal circuits.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study showed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected family members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory-evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I. All 3 developed hand tremor and upper-limb myoclonus after 1.5 years of follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) reported an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy. Affected members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration. On neuropsychological testing, patients had visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested might be due to temporal lobe dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) reported a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. The 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age, 15 years; range, 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and arose later than the hand tremor (median age, 17 years; range, 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range, 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. The most common phenotype was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. Seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied 2 families from Tuscany. Family A was a 5-generation family with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, previously mapped to chromosome 2. Its clinical features closely resembled those of family B. In family B, all patients had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs. Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in all affected individuals and appeared between 18 and 50 years of age. The affected members were: - I:2, a 70-year-old woman with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. - II:4, an 84-year-old man with onset at age 49 years and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. - III:2, a 55-year-old woman with onset at age 28 years, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, drug-resistant focal seizures and a borderline cognitive level. - III:5, a 45-year-old man with onset at age 27 years, generalized tonic-clonic seizures and drug-resistant focal seizures. - IV:1, a 29-year-old woman with onset at age 18 years and no seizures. Epilepsy occurred in all affected individuals except IV:1. Everyone except III:2 had normal intelligence. Brain MRI was normal in II:4, III:2 and III:5. None of the patients had evidence of cardiovascular disease. Two of the oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) tabulated the clinical features of 22 FAME2 families: - Families 2 to 15 and family 22 were Italian. - Family 1 was Australian/New Zealand of European ancestry. - Family 16 was Iraqi of Sephardic Jewish ancestry. - Family 17 was Israeli of Sephardic Jewish ancestry. - Family 18 was South African of European ancestry. - Family 19 was French/Spanish. - Family 20 was French. - Family 21 was a single Syrian patient. Myoclonus/cortical tremor was present in all or nearly all studied affected members of each family. The proportion with tonic-clonic seizures varied widely, from 8 of 55 (15%) in family 1 to all affected members in several smaller families. Focal seizures were infrequent: they occurred in 2 of 55 members of family 1, 2 of 4 in family 3, 3 of 11 in family 4, 2 of 4 in family 15 and 2 of 10 in family 16, and were absent in many families. Mean or median ages at onset also varied, from 12 years in family 6 to 41 years in family 19. In family 1, the authors found evidence of anticipation. Median age at onset was 30 years in generation III (range, 14-60 years; n = 6), 17 years in generation IV (range, 8-50 years; n = 30) and 12 years in generation V (range, 4-19 years; n = 16).

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) performed whole-genome sequencing in affected members of 3 FAME families and analyzed the data with ExpansionHunter and exSTRa. Within the FAME2 interval on chromosome 2, they identified an expansion of the endogenous ATTTT repeat with an inserted ATTTC repeat in the first intron of the STARD7 gene. The ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data of 69 controls. Corbett et al. (2019) then developed a repeat-primed PCR assay. With it, they identified the expansion in all 137 affected individuals from 16 independently reported FAME2 families worldwide. Overall, the expansion segregated in 158 of 158 affected individuals from 22 FAME pedigrees. Two of 24 tested individuals without a FAME diagnosis carried the expansion and were likely presymptomatic. The expansion was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples. Among family members with an uncertain diagnosis of FAME, usually tremor alone, 8 of 13 carried the expansion. In family 1, 2 tested-negative individuals with an uncertain diagnosis did not share the affected haplotype. The 20 familial cases and 52 singleton cases screened included 52 unrelated patients with generalized epilepsy and tremor or adult-onset myoclonic epilepsy. All 20 familial cases were positive, but only 1 of the 52 singleton cases was. Long-read sequencing by Corbett et al. (2019) showed that the pathogenic allele had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n. In 1 patient, a SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, while a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, suggesting somatic variation in repeat size. In another patient (family 5, III-37), a single nanopore read spanned the expanded repeats, with 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats and a total length of 4,645 bp. Two of the families with the STARD7 expansion (families 4 and 15) also carried the ADRA2B variant previously reported by De Fusco et al. (2014). Corbett et al. (2019) concluded that this strongly suggested that the ADRA2B allele is not causative.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied the variant ADRA2B receptor (alpha-2B-AR) in transfected HeLa cells. Like the wildtype receptor, the mutant localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized in an arrestin-3-dependent manner. In coimmunoprecipitation studies, however, it failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin. After 10 minutes of epinephrine stimulation, spinophilin binding to the mutant fell back to baseline, whereas binding to wildtype remained elevated. In Xenopus oocytes, spinophilin increased the EC50 for epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling through the wildtype receptor but not through the mutant. The authors concluded that the mutation increases the intensity of Ca(2+) signaling, a gain-of-function effect caused by loss of the spinophilin interaction. They proposed that the resulting cortical hyperexcitability might stem from impaired GABAergic inhibition. This ADRA2B variant was later considered not causative by Corbett et al. (2019).

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 2 Tuscan families with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME), De Fusco et al. (2014) identified an in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene: c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG; p.His225_Leu229delinsGlnPheGlyArg. The change replaced 5 amino acids (HGGAL) with 4 new ones (QFGR). In family A, the variant was heterozygous, segregated completely with the disease, and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls and public databases. The 2 families shared the disease haplotype across the critical region. Functional studies showed that the mutant receptor failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin and lost spinophilin modulation of epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling. The authors interpreted this as a gain-of-function effect.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) identified an expansion of the endogenous ATTTT repeat, with an inserted ATTTC repeat, in the first intron of the STARD7 gene. They found it by whole-genome sequencing in affected members of 3 FAME families, and it was absent from 69 control genomes. By repeat-primed PCR, the expansion segregated in 158 of 158 affected individuals from 22 FAME pedigrees. These pedigrees were of Italian, Australian/New Zealand and South African European, Sephardic Jewish (Iraqi and Israeli), French/Spanish and French ancestry. The expansion was also found in 1 Syrian singleton patient, but not in 28 control DNA samples. Long-read sequencing showed that the expanded allele had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n. In 1 patient (family 5, III-37), the allele contained 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, a total length of 4,645 bp. In another patient, reads differed in repeat number, suggesting somatic variation. STARD7 transcript and protein levels were not altered in patient fibroblasts.

checks.evidence_quote: This revealed an expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat in the context of the reverse strand of chr2 within the first intron of STARD7

checks.claim: The STARD7 expansion was found in 1 Syrian singleton patient.
checks.evidence_quote: Of these, 20/20 familial and 1/52 singleton cases were positive for an ATTTC expansion in STARD7 (Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 2; Families 2, 7, 11, 17, 18 and 21 [singleton case])

checks.claim: The STARD7 expansion was not found in 28 control DNA samples.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC repeat expansion did not amplify in any of 28 control DNA samples extracted from unaffected individuals unrelated to FAME.

checks.claim: Long-read sequencing showed that the expanded STARD7 allele had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n.
checks.evidence_quote: This suggested the structure of the pathogenic repeat in the context of the forward strand of chr2 was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n
checks.explanation: The formula was inferred from RP-PCR and includes an [N] spacer. Long-read sequencing only confirmed that the reads were made of AAATG and AAAAT repeats.

checks.explanation: Stated directly, based on a single nanopore read.

checks.claim: In another patient, sequencing reads of the STARD7 expansion differed in repeat number, suggesting somatic variation.
checks.evidence_quote: The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions, suggesting somatic variation of repeat sizes may occur within the one individual.
